Where it began

Ian Bishop was born in Port of Spain, Trinidad, on 24 October 1967. He grew into a right-arm fast bowler and made his way into the great West Indies sides of his day, playing his first Test in 1989.

The player

He was quick, among the fastest in the world at his peak, and he could move the ball away from the bat. That combination brought wickets at a startling rate. His hundredth Test wicket arrived in just his 21st match, a pace few fast bowlers have matched.

Between 1989 and 1998 he played 43 Tests and took 161 wickets at 24.29, with six five-wicket innings and a best of 6 for 40. He played one-day internationals for the West Indies too, between 1988 and 1998.

What made him special

Speed with skill, and resilience. Back trouble kept him out more than once, but each time he rebuilt his action and came back, first late in 1992 and then again in 1995. Those spells away cost him a few years, yet his record stands up beside anyone's of his time.

His batting was more for enjoyment. He made 632 Test runs at 12.15, with a best of 48. Two more blows and the scorebook would have recorded a fifty, and he would never have let his teammates forget it.

Away from the middle

After cricket he found a second career that made him just as well known. He became a commentator who followed the game around the world, and between stints in the box he completed an MBA. He also studied at the University of Leicester.

He was on the microphone when the West Indies won the Champions Trophy final in 2004 and the World Twenty20 finals of 2012 and 2016. His call of the 2016 final, as Carlos Brathwaite won it with four sixes in a row, is remembered as one of the great moments in cricket commentary. Away from cricket he follows Manchester United and loves the NBA.

And finally

Fast bowlers are usually remembered for what they did to batsmen. Bishop managed to be remembered for that and for what he said about one, which is a rare double.
